title: Line complications during outpatient parenteral antibiotic therapy: patients, lines and home care arrangements
subtitle: Design not yet settled: record review, interviews or both
statement: An OPAT service sends about 380 patients a year home with a PICC or midline, and line problems are its most common reason for unplanned returns: 41 emergency visits for line problems last year and three line-related bloodstream infections. It is not known which patients, line types or home care arrangements account for these problems, and some problems may be handled at home without reaching hospital records. The service needs to know where to act first: line choice, patient teaching or the agency's care.
whoAffected: Adults receiving intravenous antibiotics at home, their family carers, the home infusion agency's nurses, the vascular access team and the OPAT physicians.
whatHurts: Blocked, infected, thrombosed or dislodged lines interrupt treatment, bring patients back to the emergency department and can cause bloodstream infection; patients describe the line as a constant worry.
currentPractice: PICCs and midlines are chosen by the referring team and the vascular access nurse; the agency visits daily or three times a week under its own line care orders; problems are escalated case by case, and no one reviews complications across patients.
whyNow: A year with 41 emergency visits for line problems, three bloodstream infections, and linked hospital records that already cover five years.
constraints: No research funding beyond the OPAT service budget of 6,000 for this work; about 60 hours of an infectious diseases fellow's time over six months; the home infusion agency is an external contractor with its own records.
patientCenteredGoal: Patients finish their home antibiotic course without a line problem that sends them back to hospital, and know what to do when a line starts to fail.
summary: Problem framed; the design is left unresolved between a record review and interviews until the evidence and the data are reviewed.
